facts.reason: The '30 inches on the control side' setback is a Seattle amendment, not model IFGC text. Seattle's 2021 Fuel Gas Code tags 303.7 with [S] (its Seattle-amendment marker, used on 301.1, 301.6, 618.3, etc.), and the model text (e.g., 2012 NC Fuel Gas Code reproduction of IFGC 303.7) has only the 12 in setback, the 4 in masonry lining above grade and flood protection.

fixed.fact: Under IFGC 2021 303.7, an appliance installed in a pit or excavation may not touch the surrounding soil, and the pit sides must be held back at least 12 inches from the appliance. Where the pit is more than 12 inches deep below adjoining grade, its walls must be lined with concrete or masonry that extends at least 4 inches above grade and resists collapse, and the appliance must be protected from flooding.
fixed.note: Seattle's local code adds a 30-inch control-side setback ([S] amendment); that is not in the model IFGC.

facts.reason: Correct as far as it goes, but omits the commonly tested limit on the arc-resistant option: per 2021 IFGC 310.3 (Seattle 2021 SFGC text, untagged) and ICC CodeNotes on 2021 CSST bonding, if any segment of the system is non-arc-resistant CSST (or no appliance has an equipment grounding conductor), the system must be bonded per 310.2.

fixed.fact: In the 2021 IFGC, CSST that is not listed with an arc-resistant jacket must be bonded to the electrical service grounding electrode system (or lightning protection electrode system) with a jumper of at least 6 AWG copper, no longer than 75 ft, using UL 467 listed clamps (310.2). Arc-resistant CSST (ARCSST) only has to be electrically continuous and bonded to an effective ground-fault current path like other gas piping (310.3), but if any part of the system is non-arc-resistant CSST, the 310.2 direct-bond jumper is required.

facts.reason: Table 503.4 does not assign UL 1738 special gas vents to Category II/III appliances; it says Category II, III and IV appliances are vented 'as specified or furnished by manufacturers of listed appliances'. The plastic-pipe rule is in 503.4.1 (which Seattle amends, [S]); model text requires the appliance to be listed for plastic venting, the instructions to name the material, and the pipe to be labeled to the appliance maker's specified standard or listed to UL 1738.

fixed.fact: Under the 2021 IFGC, Category II, III and IV appliances are vented with the system specified or furnished by the listed appliance's manufacturer (Table 503.4); special gas vents must be listed to UL 1738 (503.4.2), and Type B and BW vents are listed to UL 441. Where plastic pipe is used, the appliance must be listed for it, its instructions must name the specific plastic material, and the pipe must be labeled to the standard the appliance manufacturer specifies or listed to UL 1738 (503.4.1). Any required primer must be a contrasting color so joints can be inspected (503.4.1.1).

facts.reason: Wrong example. R-123 boils at about 82 F at atmospheric pressure, so it is in the 'at or below 85 F' group, where nitrogen or other methods needing later purging may not be used. The 'above 85 F' group is refrigerants like R-113 (boils about 118 F). Rule text confirmed on eCFR 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii).

fixed.fact: Under 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), for a non-major repair, a low-pressure appliance must be pressurized to no higher than 0 psig before opening. For refrigerants that boil at or below 85 F at 29.9 in. Hg (such as R-11 and R-123), methods that require later purging, such as nitrogen, may not be used. For refrigerants that boil above 85 F (such as R-113), heat should be used to raise the pressure, and nitrogen may be used only to raise the pressure from the level heat can reach up to atmospheric.

facts.reason: Facts are right, but the second sentence (sale to another owner requires reclamation by a certified reclaimer) comes from 40 CFR 82.154(d) 'Sale of used refrigerant' and the 82.152 definition of reclaim (AHRI 700), not 82.156(h). Verified on eCFR.

The 'same method' rule is per operating facility, not across all of an owner's facilities. 40 CFR 84.102 (leak rate definition, eCFR): 'The same method must be used for all appliances subject to the leak repair requirements located at an operating facility.' Other values (quarterly/annual inspections, 125 percent chronic leaker report by March 1, January 1, 2026 start) confirmed on eCFR 84.106.

fixed.fact: Under the HFC leak repair rule (40 CFR 84.106, effective January 1, 2026), owners calculate the leak rate each time refrigerant is added using either the annualizing method or the rolling average method, and the same method must be used for all covered appliances at an operating facility. After an exceedance, commercial refrigeration and industrial process systems of 500 lb or more get quarterly leak inspections, while those of 15 to under 500 lb and comfort cooling systems get annual inspections, and any appliance of 15 lb or more that leaks 125 percent of its charge in a calendar year must be reported to EPA by March 1 of the next year.

facts.reason: 84.54(b) runs from each subsector's compliance date in paragraph (a), not from the product's manufacture date: 'Effective three years after the dates listed for each subsector in paragraph (a)...' (40 CFR 84.54(b), eCFR/LII).

fixed.fact: Under 40 CFR 84.54(a), since January 1, 2025 self-contained residential and light commercial AC and heat pumps, residential dehumidifiers and comfort-cooling chillers may not be manufactured or imported with refrigerant of GWP 700 or more, and household refrigerators and freezers are limited to GWP below 150. Under 84.54(b), starting three years after each of those compliance dates (January 1, 2028 for products with a January 1, 2025 date), no one may sell, distribute, offer for sale or export products that use the restricted refrigerants.

facts.reason: Misleading by omission: Manual S is also an ANSI standard (ANSI/ACCA 3 Manual S), alongside ANSI/ACCA 1 Manual D and ANSI/ACCA 2 Manual J. Saying only J and D are ANSI-approved is wrong.

fixed.fact: ACCA manuals: Manual J = residential load calculation, Manual S = residential equipment selection, Manual D = residential duct design, Manual T = air distribution basics (choosing supply outlets and returns to avoid drafts and stagnant air), Manual N = commercial load calculation, Manual Q = commercial low-pressure duct design, Manual Zr = residential zoning, Manual B = testing, adjusting and balancing, Manual H = heat pump systems, and Manual P = psychrometrics. Manuals J, S and D are ANSI-approved standards (ANSI/ACCA 2, 3 and 1).

facts.reason: Numbers are right (16 x 1.75 = 28 A; 16 x 2.25 = 36 A) but students may round up: NEC 440.22(A) sets a maximum and, unlike 430.52, has no next-higher-standard-size allowance, so the breaker is the next standard size at or below the limit. Also the limit is based on RLA or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater.

fixed.fact: Under NEC 440.22(A), the branch-circuit fuse or breaker for a hermetic motor-compressor may not exceed 175 percent of its rated-load current (or branch-circuit selection current, if greater), and may be raised to no more than 225 percent if the motor will not start; there is no round-up to the next standard size. Example: a 16 A RLA compressor allows at most 28 A (a 25 A standard breaker), or up to 36 A (35 A standard) if needed to start. The equipment nameplate MOCP must never be exceeded (NEC 110.3(B)).
